Trellis

A trellis guides growth without doing the growing. Trellis does the same for an AI that writes code: it declares up front what may be touched, what must hold true, and where the work has to stop and ask.

Method · contracts and gates Vehicle · an installable plugin Autonomy · stops before the pull request
The problem

Drift, not incompetence

When AI-assisted development fails, it is almost never because the model could not write the code. It fails through drift: work that is reasonable up close and wrong from a distance.

You ask for one thing and get something adjacent. It edits a file "while it was in there", resolves an ambiguous requirement in its own favour, or relaxes the definition of done until it matches what it built. Every individual decision makes sense. The sum does not.

Drift is not fixed by asking more nicely. It is fixed by making "what I asked for" a document a machine can check, instead of a sentence in a chat that nobody reads again.

The core

Everything else follows from two ideas

1 · The unit of work is a contract, not a prompt

A contract is a file. It declares which files may be modified, what it depends on, what may run beside it, and how — with commands — anyone can tell it is done.

That single file does four jobs at once: it is the scheduler (what can run with what), the brief handed to whoever executes, the rubric the reviewer grades against, and the record of what was agreed. When those four live in separate documents, they drift apart.

2 · A rule is enforced at the earliest tier that can express it

A rule written in a document depends on the model reading it and remembering it. The same rule turned into a hook or a test depends on nothing: the model simply cannot get past it.

So Trellis ranks the mechanisms by strength, and treats any rule living higher than it needs to as technical debt.

Anatomy

Three layers, versioned separately

Confusing them is the mistake that ends in eight diverging copies of the same framework.

The method is the idea, and it gets documented. The plugin is the vehicle, and it gets installed. The profile is each repository's calibration: build and test commands, base branch, paths, autonomy level.

From which comes the rule that prevents forks: what you tune per project is the profile, never the plugin. If you catch yourself editing the plugin to fit a repo, what is missing is a field in the profile — and that is the bug.

The lifecycle

Who decides what, and when

This is the diagram worth understanding even if nothing else lands. The top lane is what a person decides; the bottom lane is what the AI executes.

The two points where work rises into the human lane are not optional reviews. They are stops. The AI does not continue past either one on its own.

Why a failure is never retried automatically

A failed criterion marks the contract blocked and hands the decision to a person: retry with a refinement, abandon, or pause. Contracts that depended on it do not start.

Auto-retry is tempting and is exactly how the mess accumulates: three silent attempts later the tree is in a state nobody understands and the record of what was tried no longer exists.

The central piece

Inside a contract

It is a text file with a data header and a prose body. The machine reads the header; whoever executes reads the body. 

---
id: SPEC-T-01                # unique across the whole repository
status: pending               # pending · active · blocked · gated · completed · withdrawn
executor: subagent            # subagent for short work · session above ~3h or across layers
estimate: 90min

depends_on: []               # contracts that must be completed first
parallel_safe_with: []       # what may run alongside (an assertion, not a proof)
reads:                        # what it may read without modifying
  - src/App/Features/Shared/
writes:                       # ← the only paths it is allowed to modify
  - src/App/Features/Thing/
  - tests/unit/App.Tests/Features/Thing/

gates: none                    # human stops this contract expects — or `none`, stated
---

## Objective      what is true when this is done that is not true now
## Constraints    the rules that apply, copied verbatim into the brief
## Steps          the steps
## Done when      criteria — runnable commands wherever a command can express them
  - [ ] `dotnet build App.sln` exits 0
  - [ ] `dotnet test --filter Thing` exits 0
## Out of scope   what a reader might expect here and will not get, and why

The three rules that make this work

  • The contract is immutable during execution. An executor never edits its own writes, constraints or done_when. Amending the rubric you are graded against is not a shortcut, it is a categorical defect. A wrong contract is fixed by a human, in a separate commit, before code is written.
  • A declared none is a decision; an omitted field is a gap. Where the answer is "nothing", write nothing down explicitly and say why. Silence does not distinguish "not applicable" from "forgot".
  • A criterion that cannot be executed is a defect in the contract, not a step to skip when you reach it.

writes is what decides parallelism

Here is the mechanism that makes it safe to run several tasks at once. Two contracts conflict when their writes sets overlap and neither names the other as safe. Overlap is compared by path segment, not by text.

The wave

Some questions a contract cannot answer

The test is mechanical: if a contract cannot satisfy it alone, it is not the contract's to answer. It belongs to the spec — which is the wave.

A frontend contract and a backend contract each deliver half a flow. An end-to-end criterion written into either one can only fail until the other lands, or be relaxed until it passes. Both outcomes are worse than not writing it. The same shape appears for feature flags, which wrap a capability rather than a file, and for environment ceilings — one contract cannot know what the other three will be holding at the same time.

So templates/SPEC.md makes all three mandatory fields, on the usual terms: a declared none is an answer, an absent value is a gap.

ConcernDecided on the spec
End-to-end verificationWhat proves the whole wave, and which contract owns the test paths
Feature flagIts name, default state, kill path — and the contract that deletes it
Environment ceilingsPorts, licence seats, shared databases the wave will contend for
Refused, not pending

Detecting these automatically is rejected on the merits. Whether a change needs a flag is a judgement about the domain, and the structural signals a machine can read correlate weakly with the answer — so a detector is wrong most often on exactly the changes that matter, and a guardrail that cries wolf gets switched off. The framework makes the question unforgettable; it does not answer it.

A flag also never outlives its purpose by default: it is created with an owner, an expiry and the contract that removes it. The expensive failure has never been adding flags — it is the two hundred nobody dares delete.

The red line

What an agent never decides

This list is closed and does not care how green the build is. An executor that reaches one of these stops and asks.

  • Pushing to a protected branch, opening or merging a PR, any deploy.
  • Touching anything shared that other code depends on — a port interface, a shared host or bootstrap, a published schema.
  • Weakening an isolation or security control.
  • A contradiction between the contract and the code as built.
  • A decision whose wrong answer means throwing the work away.
The principle

Waiting costs nothing; guessing costs the task.

One narrow delegation

A contract a human has explicitly granted autonomy — in a repository whose profile permits it, on a base branch with required status checks — may push its task branch, open a pull request and request auto-merge. It still never merges: gh pr merge --auto asks the platform to merge if its checks pass, so the decision moves from a person remembering to look to a check that cannot be skipped. A bare merge stays denied at every level.

The grant is answered by a human before the branch exists and recorded in the contract, which is immutable during execution — so an executor cannot grant itself autonomy. Where a merge deploys to production, or the change touches a schema, a shared interface, a security control or a feature flag, it stays human whatever the profile says.

What exists and what does not, yet

What installing it does today

The plugin declares four hooks and no skills or agents — verified with claude plugin details. The hooks are the part that enforces: write boundary, git boundary, Stop gate and per-file lint. They are inert in any repository without a .trellis/profile.yml, so installing it cannot disturb work that has not opted in.

The CLI reports them as harness-only — no model context cost. That is the enforcement ladder measured rather than argued: the same rule as prose in rules/core.md is paid for in every session in the repo.

What is still prose is the part that needs roles to exist: the analyst that produces a spec and stops dead at a human gate, and the implementer that executes an approved one. Those are the next increment.

Installation

How a Claude Code plugin gets installed

There are two paths, and they serve different purposes. The first is for working on the plugin; the second is for handing it to the team.

Every command below was verified against CLI version 2.1.234. The only prerequisite is Node on the PATH — the hooks and the validator are plain Node ESM with no dependencies, so there is no build step, no bundle and no installer. A plugin is distributed as its source.

Path A · for developing it

Link it as a skills directory

Claude Code auto-loads any plugin it finds in ~/.claude/skills/. No marketplace, no install step, nothing to version: one symlink and it is there in the next session. 

git clone https://github.com/yainierc/trellis.git ~/src/trellis
ln -s ~/src/trellis ~/.claude/skills/trellis

To confirm it is seen:

claude plugin details trellis@skills-dir

The @source suffix matters here. A bare claude plugin details trellis also works, but it resolves to whichever copy is active — and a plugin installed from a marketplace shadows the one you are editing, so the bare form will happily report on a frozen snapshot while your changes sit undiscovered on disk.

Edit a file in the repo and the change is live in the next session. This is the right mode while the plugin changes daily. To remove it: rm ~/.claude/skills/trellis.

Path B · for the team

Publish it as a marketplace

A marketplace is a catalogue: a JSON file listing which plugins exist and where. It can live in the Trellis repo itself. Add .claude-plugin/marketplace.json: 

{
  "name": "gmstek",
  "description": "Claude Code plugins from GMSTEK.",
  "owner": { "name": "GMSTEK" },
  "plugins": [
    { "name": "trellis", "source": "./" }
  ]
}

Then each teammate runs, once:

claude plugin marketplace add yainierc/trellis
claude plugin install trellis@gmstek

With --scope project the marketplace is written to the repository's own .claude/settings.json as extraKnownMarketplaces, so it travels with the project instead of being added person by person.

Validate before publishing anything

The CLI checks that the manifest is well formed. Against the current Trellis manifest it already passes clean: 

claude plugin validate ~/src/trellis
✔ Validation passed

Releasing a change

The install cache is keyed by version, and this is the one operational trap worth knowing before the team depends on it: pushing new commits without touching version in plugin.json leaves everyone on the old code. claude plugin update resolves against the declared version, so it reports the plugin as up to date and pulls nothing — the new commits are simply never fetched.

So every release bumps the version, and claude plugin tag creates the trellis--vX.Y.Z tag while checking that plugin.json and the marketplace entry agree about it: 

claude plugin tag --dry-run          # check before committing to it
claude plugin tag --push
Where it lives

github.com/yainierc/trellis, public and MIT. Releases are tagged trellis--vX.Y.Z. Anything reaching installed users needs a version bump first — see below.

Getting started

Using it in a repository

All of this works today, without waiting for the hooks. The method starts paying as soon as the first well-written contract exists.

  1. Copy the profile into the target repository

    mkdir -p .trellis
cp $TRELLIS/templates/project-profile.yml .trellis/profile.yml

  2. Fill in that repo's real commands

    Build, fast tests, lint, base branch. Anything that does not apply is marked ~, which means "there is none here" — and the gate that would have used it is skipped while saying so, never silently.

  3. Write the first contract

    Copy templates/CONTRACT.md and fill it in for a small, real piece of work. The part that costs the most and returns the most is done_when: it forces you to decide, before any code is written, how "done" will be checked.

  4. Validate it

    No dependencies — Node is all you need:

    node $TRELLIS/scripts/validate-contract.mjs docs/contracts/SPEC-T-01.md

    Run it over the whole directory with --all to add the cross-contract checks: dependency cycles, references to contracts that do not exist, and writes overlaps between two contracts that declare each other safe. 

    node $TRELLIS/scripts/validate-contract.mjs docs/contracts --all

  5. Execute it, and do not believe the report

    Hand the contract to a session or a subagent on a task/<id>-<slug> branch — that branch name is how every hook knows which contract it is enforcing. From there the write boundary, the git boundary and the Stop gate apply on their own.

Maintenance

Signals that the framework is decaying

These are leading indicators. Any one of them is a reason to pause product work and repair the loop.

  • A contract reported complete left the build or tests broken → the done_when set is insufficient.
  • One session discovered a convention and the next ignored it → the learning loop is broken.
  • Two contracts declared each other safe and collided at merge → writes is under-declared; widen it, do not loosen the check.
  • A rule keeps being restated in prompts because it keeps being violated → it belongs lower on the ladder.
  • Memory and rule files only ever grow → nothing is being pruned, and context cost rises for every session in the repo.
  • A human re-reviews the same class of defect every week → that defect class needs a gate, not more review.
Institutional memory

When a real failure costs real time, its symptom, cause and fix are recorded with the date in the skill that allowed it. That table is what stops the next session from tripping the same wire, and it is never trimmed for tidiness.

Glossary

The terms, in plain words

Contract
A file declaring what may be touched, what must hold, and how it is checked. The unit of work.
Spec
The document that turns "I want X" into concrete acceptance criteria. Approved before any code is written.
Gate
A mandatory stop where a person decides. Not an after-the-fact review: the work does not move until there is an answer.
Hook
A check the system runs automatically before or after an action. The model can neither skip nor forget it.
Skill
A procedure written once so it is not re-improvised each session. Invoked as /trellis:something.
Agent
A role with a tool set and a stopping condition: the one that analyses, the one that implements, the one that reviews.
Subagent
A task running in the background with its own context. For short work; long work asks for a dedicated session.
Worktree
An isolated copy of the repository for a single task. A failed experiment gets deleted instead of unwound.
Adversarial review
A reviewer explicitly briefed to refute the work, with no access to the author's report. Only artifacts count.
Drift
Work that is locally reasonable and globally wrong. The failure mode that gives everything above its purpose.
ADR
The record of a decision taken. A recorded decision is not relitigated without a new ADR — and what was refused is recorded as refused, with its reason.
